kurals.tamil:
வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக ஓம்பா
மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை.
kurals.transliteration:
Valiyaarkku maaretral ombuka ombaa
meliyaarmel meka pakai.
kurals.meaning: Refrain from setting yourself against those stronger than you; but do not shrink from taking up enmity against those who are weaker.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a small boat and a giant ship. A smart small boat does not try to bump the giant ship, because it would sink. Valluvar says: pick your contests wisely, and never start a fight you cannot possibly win.
kurals.university: The chapter title pakai maatchi (பகை மாட்சி) means the ‘excellence’ or right conduct of enmity: not whether a ruler will have enemies, but which enmities are worth having. The couplet turns on a deliberate wordplay between ombuka (ஓம்புக, ‘guard against, avoid’) and ombaa (ஓம்பா, ‘without avoiding’), and on meka (மேக, from mevu, ‘desire, take up’). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read it as plain statecraft: avoid opposing the stronger, and willingly take up enmity against the weaker; Solomon Pappaiah sharpens it to ‘if weaker, attack at once’. Mu. Karunanidhi (Kalaignar) notably inverts the moral, praising the one who spares the weak and fights the strong as the true glory of enmity, a modern ethical rereading rather than the traditional gloss. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthashastra (Book 7) lays down the basic rule of interstate policy: a king who is inferior in power to another should make peace with him, while one who is superior should make war.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra treats war and peace as calculations of relative strength rather than matters of pride.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the same rule as the Kural: avoid the stronger, take on the weaker.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical statecraft principle from the same Indian political-science tradition; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a sensible king who measures his strength before battle and seeks peace if he is outnumbered.
christianity.tie_back: The weaker king in the parable does exactly what Valluvar advises: he does not challenge the stronger.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong practical match, though Jesus uses it as an illustration of counting the cost of discipleship.

islam.quote_or_event: At Hudaybiyyah (628 CE) the Prophet Muhammad accepted a treaty with the Quraysh on terms many of his companions felt were unfavourable, choosing a truce over a confrontation at that moment.
islam.explanation: The early Muslim community, not yet in a position to prevail at Mecca, accepted peace, and the truce later opened the way to its growth.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows the wisdom of not pressing a contest at an unfavourable moment.
islam.source: Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari 2731-2732 (Book of Conditions)
islam._accuracy_note: Partial match: Islamic sources frame the treaty as divine wisdom and patience, not simply as a strength calculation.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jeremiah urges King Zedekiah to submit to the yoke of the king of Babylon and live, rather than rebel against an overwhelmingly stronger empire; Zedekiah’s revolt ends in the fall of Jerusalem.
judaism.explanation: The prophet counsels against defying a power that cannot be resisted, and the king who ignored him brought ruin on his city.
judaism.tie_back: It is a tragic illustration of the first half of the Kural: do not set yourself against the stronger.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good situational match, though Jeremiah’s reason is theological (Babylon as God’s instrument), not prudence alone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that victory breeds enmity and the defeated live in pain, while the peaceful live happily, having given up both victory and defeat.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha looks past the calculation of winning and losing to the suffering that every conflict produces.
buddhism.tie_back: It offers a contrasting view: where Valluvar teaches which fights to pick, the Buddha questions picking fights at all.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Contrast rather than parallel; Buddhism has no direct counterpart to choosing weaker enemies.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Melian Dialogue the Athenian envoys tell the people of Melos that, between unequal powers, the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must; Melos resists and is destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Thucydides dramatises the harsh logic of power: a small state that defies a great one is crushed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Melos is the classic case of a weaker party ignoring the Kural’s first warning.
greek_mythology.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 5.84-116
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Historical (not mythological) Greek source, but an exact thematic match on the strong-versus-weak calculus.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu advises that a general equal in strength may give battle, one slightly inferior should avoid the enemy, and one unequal in every way should withdraw.
philosophy.explanation: The Art of War makes the decision to fight depend entirely on a sober comparison of forces.
philosophy.tie_back: Sun Tzu and Valluvar give the same rule: never engage a stronger foe.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War III.9-10 (tr. Lionel Giles)

kurals.tamil:
அன்பிலன் ஆன்ற துணையிலன் தான்துவ்வான்
என்பரியும் ஏதிலான் துப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbilan aandra thunaiyilan thaanthuvvaan
enpariyum edhilaan thuppu.
kurals.meaning: One who has no love for his own people, no strong allies, and no strength of his own: how could he ever break the power of an enemy?
kurals.elementary: Think of a team captain who is mean to his teammates, has no friends on other teams to help, and is not a strong player himself. When a tough team shows up, how can he possibly win? Kindness, friends and your own strength are what keep you safe.
kurals.university: The couplet lists three deficits: anbilan (அன்பிலன், without love, which Pappaiah and Varadarasanar read as lacking affection for kin and subjects), aandra thunaiyilan (ஆன்ற துணையிலன், without worthy or powerful allies) and thaan thuvvaan (தான் துவ்வான், himself lacking strength). The closing phrase enpariyum edhilaan thuppu (என் பரியும் ஏதிலான் துப்பு) asks how such a man could destroy (pari) the strength (thuppu) of a stranger-foe (edhilaan). Parimelazhagar reads the verse as the converse of 861: such a person is himself the ‘weak’ party whom others may safely oppose. The trio of affection, alliance and own strength mirrors the Arthashastra’s concern with internal loyalty and allies (mitra) as elements of royal power. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Arthashastra names the seven constituent elements of a state (the king, ministers, country, fort, treasury, army and ally) and treats a ruler lacking loyal subjects and allies as easily overthrown.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya sees power as a combination of personal capacity, popular loyalty and alliances.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s three deficits (no love, no allies, no strength) are the same missing elements.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good structural match on allies and strength; the ‘love’ element is implicit in Kautilya rather than explicit.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul writes that even if he had prophecy, all knowledge and faith to move mountains, without charity (love) he would be nothing.
christianity.explanation: For Paul, love is not an extra but the thing that gives every other gift its worth.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar likewise puts love (anbu) first among the things without which a person is powerless.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared emphasis on love, but Paul speaks of spiritual worth, not political or military strength.

islam.quote_or_event: “And obey Allāh and His Messenger, and do not dispute and [thus] lose courage and [then] your strength would depart; and be patient. Indeed, Allāh is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns a community facing enemies that internal quarrelling drains away both courage and strength.
islam.tie_back: Both texts tie a group’s power against foes to the bonds within it.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on loss of strength through lack of internal bonds; context is the believing community at war.

judaism.quote_or_event: Kohelet observes that two are better than one, that woe comes to the one who falls alone with no one to lift him, and that a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
judaism.explanation: The sage notes, in simple human terms, that a person without companions is vulnerable.
judaism.tie_back: It echoes Valluvar’s friendless man who cannot withstand an enemy.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on allies; less on the ‘love’ and ‘own strength’ elements.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Ananda suggests that admirable friendship is half the holy life, the Buddha corrects him: it is the whole of the holy life.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats good companionship as essential, not optional, for spiritual progress.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar too treats worthy companions as indispensable, though for worldly survival.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shared value on companions, but the Buddhist context is spiritual practice, not conflict.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the father and his quarrelling sons, he shows them that a bundle of sticks cannot be broken while single sticks snap easily.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable teaches that unity makes a family strong and division makes each member easy to defeat.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar’s loveless, ally-less man is the single stick.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Father and His Sons’
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear parallel on unity and allies; a fable rather than myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli advises that the best fortress a prince can have is not to be hated by his people, since walls will not save a ruler whose subjects turn against him.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli, the loyalty of one’s own people is a more reliable defence than any fortification.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise makes affection for one’s own people the first line of defence.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 20 (tr. W. K. Marriott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on internal loyalty as strength; paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
அஞ்சும் அறியான் அமைவிலன் ஈகலான்
தஞ்சம் எளியன் பகைக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anjum ariyaan amaivilan eekalaan
thanjam eliyan pakaikku.
kurals.meaning: A man who is fearful, ignorant, unable to get along with others and unwilling to give is utterly easy prey for his enemies.
kurals.elementary: Picture a kid who is scared of everything, doesn’t learn the rules of the game, won’t cooperate with anyone, and never shares. When trouble comes, nobody stands with him and he doesn’t know what to do. Being brave, learning, getting along and sharing are what make you strong.
kurals.university: Four faults are stacked in quick succession: anjum (அஞ்சும், he who fears, which Pappaiah glosses as fearing what need not be feared), ariyaan (அறியான், one who does not know what should be known), amaivilan (அமைவிலன், lacking accord or adaptability with others) and eekalaan (ஈகலான், one who does not give). Thanjam (தஞ்சம்) is read by the commentators as an intensifier, ‘very easily’ (Varadarasanar: மிக எளியவன்). Parimelazhagar’s logic is cumulative: fear loses battles, ignorance loses policy, unsociability loses allies and stinginess loses the army, so the foe has little left to overcome. Kalaignar renders amaivilan as lacking the habit of living in harmony and eekalaan as lacking compassion. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the opening of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna rebukes the despondent Arjuna, urging him not to yield to unmanliness and to cast off his petty faint-heartedness and rise.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna treats Arjuna’s fear and confusion on the battlefield as a weakness that must be overcome before anything else.
hinduism.tie_back: Fear and not-knowing, the first two faults in the Kural, are exactly what Krishna addresses.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the fear and confusion elements; the Gita’s concern is duty, not vulnerability to enemies.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul tells Timothy that God has not given a spirit of fear, but of power, love and a sound mind.
christianity.explanation: Paul sets fear against three positive qualities that a leader of the church should have.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s fearful, unloving, ignorant man is the opposite of Paul’s ideal of power, love and a sound mind.
christianity._accuracy_note: Interesting inverse match on fear, love and sound judgement; not about enemies.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Allah! I seek refuge with You from miserliness; and seek refuge with You from cowardice; and seek refuge with You from being sent back to geriatric old age...”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught a supplication that names miserliness and cowardice side by side as evils to be protected from.
islam.tie_back: Two of the Kural’s four faults, fear and not giving, are paired in the same breath.
islam._accuracy_note: Striking pairing of cowardice and miserliness; spiritual rather than military framing.

judaism.quote_or_event: Before battle, the officers of Israel are told to send home any man who is fearful and fainthearted, lest his brothers’ hearts melt like his.
judaism.explanation: Deuteronomy treats fear as contagious and dangerous to the whole army.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural places fear first among the faults that make one easy prey.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on fear in war; covers only one of the four faults.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha names four bases of social solidarity (generosity, kind speech, beneficial help and impartiality) and says they hold the world together like the linchpin of a moving chariot.
buddhism.explanation: Without these qualities, the Buddha says, people would not respect or support one another.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ungenerous, unaccommodating man lacks exactly these bonds, which is why he stands alone.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on generosity and sociability; does not address fear or enemies.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Paris shrinks back into the ranks in fear when Menelaus steps forward, and Hector rebukes him for his cowardice.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows how a prince’s fear shames him before both armies.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris embodies the first fault of the Kural: the fearful man who cannot face his foe.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates fear only; Paris is otherwise not ignorant or stingy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness, and liberality as the mean between meanness and prodigality.
philosophy.explanation: Cowardice and meanness are, for Aristotle, vices that undermine a person’s character and standing.
philosophy.tie_back: Two of Valluvar’s four faults appear in Aristotle’s list of vices.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.6-9 and IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Conceptual overlap on vices; Aristotle is not discussing vulnerability to enemies.

kurals.tamil:
நீங்கான் வெகுளி நிறையிலன் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
யாங்கணும் யார்க்கும் எளிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Neengaan vekuli niraiyilan enjnaandrum
yaanganum yaarkkum elidhu.
kurals.meaning: One whose anger never leaves him and who has no inner restraint is easy for anyone to defeat, at any time and in any place.
kurals.elementary: If a player gets angry every time and can’t keep the team’s plan a secret, the other team just has to tease him and listen in. He makes himself easy to beat. Staying calm and keeping your plans to yourself is a kind of armour.
kurals.university: Neengaan vekuli (நீங்கான் வெகுளி) is anger that does not depart, a settled irascibility rather than a passing flare. Nirai (நிறை) is the key term: Varadarasanar glosses it as the capacity to hold and govern one’s own mind, while Parimelazhagar’s tradition, followed by Solomon Pappaiah and the classic English rendering (‘neither refrains from anger nor keeps his secrets’), reads it as guarding secrets. Both senses describe a leak in self-command through which the enemy can enter. The triple universal of the second line, enjnaandrum yaanganum yaarkkum (எஞ்ஞான்றும் யாங்கணும் யார்க்கும், at all times, in all places, to all), makes the vulnerability total. This anticipates chapter 31 (vekulaamai, avoiding anger), here recast as political danger. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna traces a chain of ruin: from anger comes delusion, from delusion confusion of memory, from that the loss of intelligence, and with intelligence lost, a person is destroyed.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita shows anger as the first link in a collapse of judgement.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s permanently angry man has lost exactly the judgement that would protect him.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close psychological match; the Gita’s concern is spiritual ruin rather than defeat by enemies.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb compares a person without self-control to an undefended city that anyone can enter.
christianity.tie_back: It is almost the Kural’s image: the man without nirai is open to any attacker.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one image of self-command as a city wall; a Hebrew Bible text shared by the Christian canon.

islam.quote_or_event: “The strong is not the one who overcomes the people by his strength, but the strong is the one who controls himself while in anger.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet redefines strength as mastery of one’s own anger.
islam.tie_back: By that measure, Valluvar’s ever-angry man is the weakest of all.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct match on anger and self-control as strength.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma asks, ‘Who is mighty?’ and answers: the one who conquers his own impulse.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah locates true power in self-mastery rather than in force.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar’s man without nirai has failed at exactly this kind of might.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on self-mastery as strength; paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada calls the one who checks rising anger as a charioteer checks a speeding chariot a true charioteer; others merely hold the reins.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises active control of anger as real mastery.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s man whose anger never leaves has let go of the reins.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on restraint of anger; paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Ajax, the hero’s rage at losing Achilles’ armour drives him into a delusion in which he slaughters livestock, believing them to be his enemies, and ends in disgrace.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ajax’s unrelenting anger destroys him more completely than any enemy could.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the Kural’s man of unrelenting anger, undone without a battle.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on anger’s self-destruction; the gods’ role in his madness complicates the parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca calls anger a brief madness, an emotion that cannot govern itself, forgets decency and is deaf to reason.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, the angry man has handed control of himself to a passion.
philosophy.tie_back: This is why Valluvar says the angry man is easy prey: he is no longer in command.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira I.1 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match on anger as loss of self-government; paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
வழிநோக்கான் வாய்ப்பன செய்யான் பழிநோக்கான்
பண்பிலன் பற்றார்க்கு இனிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Vazhinokkaan vaayppana seyyaan pazhinokkaan
panbilan patraarkku inidhu.
kurals.meaning: One who does not look to the right path, does not do what is fitting, does not care about disgrace and has no good character is a delight to his enemies.
kurals.elementary: A kid who never reads the rules, doesn’t do his homework, doesn’t care if people think badly of him and isn’t kind is very easy for a rival to beat. His rival is actually happy to face him! Learning the right way and caring about your good name make you hard to beat.
kurals.university: Vazhi nokkaan (வழிநோக்கான்) is glossed by Parimelazhagar’s tradition, and by Puliyur Kesigan and Pappaiah, as one who does not study the treatises of right conduct (neethi nool); Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it more broadly as not seeking the good path. Vaayppana seyyaan (வாய்ப்பன செய்யான்) is one who fails to do what those texts enjoin or what is fitting; pazhi nokkaan (பழிநோக்கான்) disregards blame or disgrace; panbilan (பண்பிலன்) lacks character. Patraar (பற்றார்) are ‘those who do not hold to him’, that is, enemies, and inidhu (இனிது, sweet) is deliberately ironic: such a man is a pleasure to fight. The sequence moves from knowledge to action to reputation to character. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna warns that one who casts aside the injunctions of scripture and acts on impulse attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal, and therefore scripture should be one’s guide in what to do and what to avoid.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita insists that right action must be guided by authoritative teaching, not whim.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s vazhi nokkaan and vaayppana seyyaan are exactly the man who ignores such guidance.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on ignoring prescribed conduct; the Gita’s stake is spiritual, not political.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus compares the one who hears his sayings but does not do them to a foolish man who built his house on sand; when the storm came, it fell, and great was its fall.
christianity.explanation: Knowing what is right without doing it leaves a person with no foundation in a crisis.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s man who neither seeks nor does what is fitting will likewise collapse when an enemy strikes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on failure to act on right teaching; the parable is spiritual.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an speaks of those who have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see and ears with which they do not hear, calling them heedless.
islam.explanation: The verse condemns people who possess every faculty for guidance but refuse to use it.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar’s man who will not look to the right path is heedless in the same way.
islam._accuracy_note: Thematic match on wilful heedlessness; no link to enemies.

judaism.quote_or_event: Hosea proclaims that the people are destroyed for lack of knowledge, because they have rejected knowledge and forgotten the teaching of their God.
judaism.explanation: The prophet links national ruin directly to the neglect of instruction.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, refusing to learn the right way leaves one open to destruction.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on neglected knowledge leading to ruin; paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada likens fine words not put into practice to a beautiful flower that has colour but no fragrance.
buddhism.explanation: Teaching is fruitless unless it is lived.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s man who does not do what is fitting is all colour and no fragrance.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Partial match on knowing without doing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says the best man is he who thinks things out for himself, the good man is he who listens to good advice, but the one who neither thinks for himself nor heeds another is useless.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod ranks people by how they relate to wisdom, and puts the one who ignores all counsel at the bottom.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar’s man who does not look to the path is Hesiod’s useless man.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on ignoring wisdom; Hesiod’s focus is livelihood, not enemies.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Your enemy, wide awake, is constantly lying in wait to take advantage of your actions, and seeking to gain some hold on you, and keeping a constant patrol about your life …”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch says an enemy watches every action for a fault to seize on, and he urges that this watchfulness be turned to profit by living so carefully that the enemy finds nothing to use.
philosophy.tie_back: Read from the other side, Plutarch's point matches the Kural's: a person who neglects right conduct, propriety and shame hands his watching enemies exactly what they want.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, How to Profit by One's Enemies (De capienda ex inimicis utilitate), ch. 3 (tr. F. C. Babbitt)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Babbitt, Loeb Moralia vol. II, 1928). Partial match: Plutarch states the positive lesson (live blamelessly because enemies are watching), whereas the Kural describes the negligent man who delights his enemies; the four specific failings are not listed.

kurals.tamil:
காணாச் சினத்தான் கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்
பேணாமை பேணப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaanaach chinaththaan kazhiperung kaamaththaan
penaamai penap padum.
kurals.meaning: The enmity of a man blinded by anger and swollen with boundless desire is something to be welcomed, because he will defeat himself.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a rival who gets so angry he can’t see straight and wants everything he sees, right now. He runs around grabbing and shouting and forgets to defend himself. Having a rival like that is almost lucky, because his own temper and greed trip him up.
kurals.university: Kaanaach chinam (காணாச் சினம்) is anger that does not see, which Puliyur Kesigan explains as anger that blinds one to oneself and to others, and Varadarasanar as anger that does not see the truth. Kazhi perung kaamam (கழிபெருங் காமம்) is desire grown beyond all measure; Pappaiah specifies it as lust for women, while Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep the broader sense of greed or great desire. The second line plays on the root penu (to cherish): penaamai (பேணாமை, non-cherishing, i.e. enmity) penap padum (பேணப் படும், will be cherished), so his hostility is ‘to be prized’ by others. The pairing of krodha and kama as twin enemies of self-government is common to classical Indian thought. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Arjuna asks what drives a man to sin against his will; Krishna answers that it is desire (kama), which turns into anger (krodha), all-devouring and the great enemy here in this world.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita names desire and anger together as the inner enemy that overpowers a person.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar names the same pair, anger and boundless desire, as what makes a man an easy foe.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on the kama-krodha pairing; the Gita’s enemy is internal and spiritual.

christianity.quote_or_event: James teaches that each person is tempted when drawn away by his own lust, and that lust, when it has conceived, brings forth sin, and sin brings forth death.
christianity.explanation: Unchecked desire leads step by step to self-destruction.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar’s man of boundless desire is on that same downward path, which is why his enmity is no threat.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the self-destructive power of desire; does not address anger or enemies.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an asks the Prophet whether he has seen the one who takes his own desire as his god, asking whether he can be a guardian over such a person.
islam.explanation: The verse portrays a person wholly ruled by desire as beyond help.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar’s man of boundless desire is likewise ruled from within, and so is easily overcome from without.
islam._accuracy_note: Thematic match on being ruled by desire; no reference to anger or enemies.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Philistine lords, unable to overcome Samson by force, use his passion for Delilah to learn the secret of his strength, and so capture him.
judaism.explanation: Samson’s enemies win not by strength but by exploiting his desire.
judaism.tie_back: This is exactly why the Kural says such a man’s enmity is to be welcomed: his passions hand his foes the victory.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close narrative illustration of desire making a strong man easy prey.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says there is no fire like lust, no grip like hatred, no net like delusion and no river like craving.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures desire and hatred as forces that seize and drag a person along.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s blind anger and boundless desire are the fire and the grip that leave a man defenceless.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on desire and hatred as overpowering; paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Paris’s desire for Helen leads him to carry her off from Sparta, bringing the Greek armies down on Troy and destroying his own city.
greek_mythology.explanation: One prince’s unchecked desire brings ruin on his whole people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris is the Kural’s man of boundless desire whose enmity his foes could welcome.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad (background) and the Trojan cycle
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration of desire’s cost; the abduction is background to, not narrated in, the Iliad.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book IX of the Republic, Plato describes the tyrannical man as ruled by a master passion, a slave to desires that multiply without limit, and therefore the most wretched and least free of men.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, the person governed by unlimited appetite is inwardly enslaved, however powerful he seems.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar sees the same inner slavery as an outward weakness enemies can exploit.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on desire as enslavement; Plato’s focus is the soul’s misery rather than military weakness.

kurals.tamil:
கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் மன்ற அடுத்திருந்து
மாணாத செய்வான் பகை.
kurals.transliteration:
Koduththum kolalvendum mandra aduththirundhu
maanaadha seyvaan pakai.
kurals.meaning: The enmity of one who stays close to you yet does what is unworthy should certainly be had, even if you must pay a price for it.
kurals.elementary: Suppose someone on your own team keeps quietly messing up every play. It would honestly be better if he went over to the other team, even if you had to give up something to make that happen. A clear opponent is safer than a teammate who harms you from inside.
kurals.university: The commentators divide on aduththirundhu (அடுத்திருந்து). Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as ‘staying close by’: one who remains near you as an associate yet does unworthy things (maanaadha, மாணாத) should be turned into an open enemy, even at the cost of wealth. The older line represented by Parimelazhagar, followed by Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan and by the classic English version (‘having begun a work, does what is not conducive’), reads it as ‘having undertaken’ an action: the enmity of a foe who mismanages his own undertakings is so advantageous that it is worth buying. Mandra (மன்ற) means ‘certainly’. Either way the paradox is that some enmity is a gain worth paying for. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata war, Shalya agrees to serve as Karna’s charioteer but undermines him throughout with discouraging and belittling speech, weakening him from within his own chariot.
hinduism.explanation: An ally placed at Karna’s side becomes a source of harm rather than help.
hinduism.tie_back: Shalya is the close companion who does unworthy things, of whom the Kural says an open enemy would be better.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Karna Parva (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit for the ‘staying close’ reading; less for Parimelazhagar’s ‘undertaking’ reading.

christianity.quote_or_event: Judas, one of the twelve, leads the arresting party to Gethsemane and identifies Jesus with a kiss; Jesus asks whether he betrays the Son of man with a kiss.
christianity.explanation: The betrayal comes from inside the closest circle, under the sign of friendship.
christianity.tie_back: Judas is the archetype of the one who stays close yet does harm.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear case of harm from a close associate, but no idea of preferring open enmity.

islam.quote_or_event: “Had they gone forth with you, they would not have increased you except in confusion, and they would have been active among you, seeking [to cause] you fitnah [i.e., chaos and dissension]. And among you are avid listeners to them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says it was better that the hypocrites stayed behind, since inside the army they would only have spread disorder.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it judges a harmful insider to be worse than his absence.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on the danger of harmful insiders; it is about their absence rather than open enmity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it: neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; then I would have hid myself from him: But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says an open enemy can be endured or avoided, but harm from a close companion cannot.
judaism.tie_back: This is the heart of the Kural’s logic: an open foe is easier to deal with than a harmful intimate.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match for the ‘staying close’ reading; quoted from the KJV rendering of the Hebrew Psalter.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, the Buddha’s cousin and a monk within the Sangha, plotted against the Buddha and caused a schism by leading away a group of monks.
buddhism.explanation: The most dangerous opposition to the Buddha arose from inside his own community.
buddhism.tie_back: Devadatta is the insider whose ‘unworthy deeds’ did more harm than any outside foe.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good case of harm from within; Buddhist texts do not advise turning him into an open enemy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Trojans bring the great wooden horse inside their walls as a gift, and the Greek warriors hidden within open the gates by night, so Troy falls.
greek_mythology.explanation: What the Trojans welcomed into their city destroyed them from within.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The horse is the danger the Kural warns of: harm lodged close by is worse than an enemy outside the walls.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Imagistic match on the enemy within; the horse is an enemy ruse, not a false ally.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli warns that auxiliary troops borrowed from another power are useless and dangerous, because if they lose you are ruined and if they win you are their captive.
philosophy.explanation: Forces that stand beside you without real loyalty are more dangerous than open enemies.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise prefers a clear enemy to a companion whose conduct harms you.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 13 (tr. W. K. Marriott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on the danger of unreliable allies; Machiavelli does not recommend buying their enmity.

kurals.tamil:
குணனிலனாய்க் குற்றம் பலவாயின் மாற்றார்க்கு
இனனிலனாம் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Gunanilanaayk kutram palavaayin maatraarkku
inanilanaam emaap pudaiththu.
kurals.meaning: A man with no virtues and many faults ends up with no allies, and that very friendlessness becomes a strength for his enemies.
kurals.elementary: If someone is never kind and always does mean things, little by little all his friends leave. When a problem comes, he is alone, and that makes it easy for anyone against him. Good habits are what keep friends by your side.
kurals.university: The couplet is a causal chain: gunanilan (குணனிலன், without good qualities) plus kutram pala (குற்றம் பல, many faults) yields inanilan (இனனிலன், one without kin or allies, from inam, ‘one’s own group’), and that condition is emaappu (ஏமாப்பு, security or advantage) for the maatraar (மாற்றார், adversaries). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both stress that it is the friendlessness itself, not any action of the foe, that becomes the enemy’s strength. Kalaignar condenses this to ‘he loses his supporters and is easily brought down’. The verse links this chapter back to the Natpiyal chapters on friendship that precede it. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Ravana scorns his brother Vibhishana’s counsel to return Sita and insults him; Vibhishana leaves Lanka and joins Rama, bringing vital knowledge of Lanka’s defences.
hinduism.explanation: Ravana’s arrogance and wrongdoing drive away his own wise kinsman, who becomes a decisive asset to the enemy.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural exactly: a faulty man loses his own people, and his loss is the foe’s gain.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-exact narrative match of faults causing loss of kin to the enemy’s advantage.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus says that if a kingdom is divided against itself it cannot stand, and if a house is divided against itself it cannot stand.
christianity.explanation: A community that loses its inner cohesion collapses.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s man who has driven away his allies stands in just such a divided house.
christianity._accuracy_note: General match on loss of cohesion; does not link it to personal faults.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allāh, [O Muḥammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the Prophet that his gentleness kept his followers together, and harshness would have scattered them.
islam.tie_back: It is the positive mirror of the Kural: good character keeps allies, bad character loses them.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct match on character holding or losing supporters.

judaism.quote_or_event: When the people ask Rehoboam to lighten their burden, he rejects the elders’ advice and answers harshly; the ten northern tribes break away and the kingdom is split.
judaism.explanation: A king’s harshness and poor judgement cost him most of his own people.
judaism.tie_back: Rehoboam shows how faults, not enemies, can leave a ruler without allies.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match on faults causing loss of support.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjians, the Buddha says they cannot be conquered so long as they meet in harmony, honour their elders and keep their customs.
buddhism.explanation: The Vajjians’ strength lies in their unity and good conduct, not in their armies.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar describes the reverse: a man whose faults have stripped him of allies has lost exactly this protection.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good inverse match on virtue and unity as protection from enemies.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Agamemnon insults Achilles by seizing his prize Briseis; Achilles withdraws from the fighting and the Trojans drive the Greeks back to their ships.
greek_mythology.explanation: A leader’s arrogance drives away his greatest ally, to the great benefit of the enemy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agamemnon’s fault turns his own camp’s loss into Troy’s advantage, as the Kural predicts.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong illustration, though Agamemnon is not a man ‘without virtues’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Therefore the bad man does not seem to be amicably disposed even to himself, because there is nothing in him to love; so that if to be thus is the height of wretchedness, we should strain every nerve to avoid wickedness and should endeavour to be good; for so and only so can one be either friendly to oneself or a friend to another.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that a wicked man, having nothing lovable in him, is at odds with himself and cannot be a true friend to others. In the next chapter he adds that bad men cannot hold together in common purpose.
philosophy.tie_back: This supports the Kural's claim that a man without virtues and full of faults ends up without allies.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, IX.4, 1166b (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross). Strong match on vice leaving a man friendless; Aristotle does not draw the Kural's further strategic conclusion that this friendlessness strengthens his enemies.

kurals.tamil:
செறுவார்க்குச் சேணிகவா இன்பம் அறிவிலா
அஞ்சும் பகைவர்ப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seruvaarkkuch chenikavaa inbam arivilaa
anjum pakaivarp perin.
kurals.meaning: Those who fight will never be far from joy if they happen to get enemies who are both foolish and fearful.
kurals.elementary: If you are playing a game and your opponent doesn’t understand the rules and is scared to make any move, winning becomes easy and fun. Valluvar says a foolish, frightened enemy is really a stroke of luck for the other side.
kurals.university: Seruvaar (செறுவார்) are those who attack or contend; sen ikavaa inbam (சேண் இகவா இன்பம்) is joy that does not go far away, i.e. abiding delight. Varadarasanar keeps this sense (pleasures will not depart), while Puliyur Kesigan reads it as ‘all lofty pleasures remain with them’. The enemy’s two qualities, arivilaa (அறிவிலா, without understanding, which Pappaiah specifies as without knowledge of what is just) and anjum (அஞ்சும், fearing), recapitulate the first two faults of 863. Kalaignar renders the joy specifically as the joy of victory. The verse is the offensive counterpart to the chapter’s earlier defensive lists. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Virata Parva, Prince Uttara boasts that he will defeat the Kaurava army alone, but on seeing it he panics and tries to flee, until Arjuna, disguised as Brihannala, takes the reins and wins the battle.
hinduism.explanation: The episode contrasts the boastful, frightened prince with the skilled warrior who routs the host.
hinduism.tie_back: Uttara is the ignorant, fearful kind of opponent whom the Kural says is a joy to face.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Go-harana) (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Illustrates a foolish and fearful fighter, though Uttara is on the winning side in the end.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus says of the blind guides of his day: if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.
christianity.explanation: Ignorance in those who lead brings ruin on them and their followers.
christianity.tie_back: A foe led by such blindness is, as the Kural says, easy to overcome.
christianity._accuracy_note: Weak parallel on ignorance leading to a fall; not about enemies or fear.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Prophet, urge the believers to battle. If there are among you twenty [who are] steadfast, they will overcome two hundred. And if there are among you one hundred [who are steadfast], they will overcome a thousand of those who have disbelieved because they are a people who do not understand.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an promises that steadfast fighters will overcome much larger forces who lack understanding.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, an enemy without understanding becomes easy to defeat.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on foes who ‘do not understand’ being overcome; the verse emphasises the believers’ steadfastness.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the covenant curses of Leviticus, God warns that a disobedient people will be so faint-hearted in the lands of their enemies that the sound of a driven leaf will put them to flight.
judaism.explanation: Fear can so paralyse a people that they flee when no one is pursuing.
judaism.tie_back: Such a fearful foe is exactly what the Kural calls a joy to the attacker.
judaism._accuracy_note: Vivid match on fearful enemies; framed as divine punishment, not strategy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes five kinds of warriors, including one who loses heart at the mere sight of the cloud of dust raised by the enemy and cannot go into battle.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta uses these timid warriors as an image for monks who give up their practice at the first sign of temptation.
buddhism.tie_back: The warrior who falters at the dust cloud is the fearful foe of the Kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the image of the fearful fighter; the sutta’s meaning is spiritual.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus outwits the brutish Cyclops Polyphemus by telling him his name is ‘Nobody’, getting him drunk and blinding him, so that when Polyphemus cries for help his neighbours hear that ‘Nobody’ is hurting him.
greek_mythology.explanation: A powerful but witless enemy is overcome by cunning.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Polyphemus is the arivilaa, the foe without understanding whose defeat is a delight.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good on the foolish foe; Polyphemus is not fearful.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu teaches that if you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles.
philosophy.explanation: Victory follows from knowledge, and an enemy without it is at a decisive disadvantage.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s ignorant foe is the one who knows neither, and so delivers victory to his opponent.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War III.18 (tr. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the knowledge element; does not address fear.

kurals.tamil:
கல்லான் வெகுளும் சிறுபொருள் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
ஒல்லானை ஒல்லா தொளி.
kurals.transliteration:
Kallaan vekulum siruporul enjnaandrum
ollaanai ollaa tholi.
kurals.meaning: The man who will not take even the small, easy gain of opposing an unlearned foe will never have glory come to him.
kurals.elementary: If you won’t even try an easy level of a game, how will you ever beat the hard ones and earn a trophy? Valluvar says that someone who shies away from small, easy challenges never earns a great name.
kurals.university: The syntax is compressed: kallaan vekulum siruporul (கல்லான் வெகுளும் சிறுபொருள்) is ‘the small gain of being angry with (fighting) the unlearned man’, and ollaanai ollaadhu oli (ஒல்லானை ஒல்லாது ஒளி) says that light, i.e. fame, will not unite with the one who does not obtain it. Varadarasanar on thirukkural.net reads: one who cannot do the easy thing of opposing the unlearned will never gain glory; Pappaiah adds that the gain from fighting one ignorant of the treatises is small, yet the king who disdains it earns no renown; Kalaignar has fame mock such a man for hesitating even before untrained foes. Note: ytamizh.com’s Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar glosses for 870 are misplaced (they discuss forgiving old friends, the theme of kural 810); the couplet text itself is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that if he refuses to fight this righteous battle he will abandon his duty and his good name, and people will speak of his dishonour for ever.
hinduism.explanation: For a warrior, shrinking from a fight he ought to take means the loss of glory.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that glory never comes to one who will not take up a fight within his reach.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on refusing battle and losing fame; Arjuna’s foes are formidable, not unlearned.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus teaches that the one who is faithful in what is least is faithful also in much, and the one unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
christianity.explanation: Small tasks are the test that qualifies a person for greater ones.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar’s man who will not take the small gain shows he is unfit for great glory.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the small-before-great logic; context is stewardship, not conflict.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, what is [the matter] with you that, when you are told to go forth in the cause of Allāh, you adhere heavily to the earth?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an rebukes those who hang back when called to act.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it faults the reluctance that forfeits honour.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches reluctance to act; the verse’s stakes are religious, not worldly fame.

judaism.quote_or_event: Hillel teaches that in a place where there are no worthy men, one should strive to be one.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah urges a person to step up when the situation calls for it, rather than hold back.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise expects the capable to take up what lies before them, or forfeit their standing.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:5 (Hillel; numbered 2:6 in some editions)
judaism._accuracy_note: Loose match on rising to the occasion; not about enemies or fame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that one who conquers himself is a greater victor than one who conquers a thousand times a thousand men in battle.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redirects the idea of glory from outer victories to inner mastery.
buddhism.tie_back: It offers a counterpoint to the Kural’s worldly calculus of fame through victory.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Contrast rather than parallel; Buddhism does not prize martial glory.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles tells the embassy that his mother foretold two fates: if he stays and fights at Troy he will die young but win undying glory; if he goes home he will live long without fame.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, glory (kleos) is won only by those who accept the fight.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar likewise says fame never comes to one who declines the contest.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Matches fame through battle; the Kural’s point about easy, small victories is absent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu says that what the ancients called a clever fighter is one who not only wins but wins with ease, by defeating an enemy already defeated.
philosophy.explanation: Strategy consists in seizing victories that are within easy reach.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise faults the man who will not take the easy win over an unlearned foe.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IV.11-13 (tr. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good match on taking easy victories; Sun Tzu notes such wins bring little fame, partly contrary to the Kural.
